Rule-Based Data Governance

data-governance-workflow.Rmd

The problem: a CSV has no schema

A CSV is just text. Whether 47401 is a ZIP code, a county FIPS, or a count is invisible to the reader — every program that opens the file has to guess, and they guess differently. datagoodr fixes this by pairing the data with a Data Governance File (DGF): a small table, one row per variable, that records how the data is stored, how it should be read, and what it means. The DGF is a rule-based artifact — you write the name of a rule in a cell, and the package applies it — so governance is declarative, portable, and reproducible.

Three stages, two bridges

A variable’s type lives on a short journey from the raw file to how you actually want to analyze it. The DGF columns are grouped to mirror that journey:

RAW CSV ──raw_to_stable_transform──▶ GOVERNED CSV ──desired_data_import_rule──▶ ANALYSIS
   │            (reformat: lossless)        │           (coerce into type)          │
 raw_*                              stable_*                               desired_*
 how R reads the raw file           the canonical current state           what it should BE
 (type, format)                     (type, format)                        (type, class)
  • raw_ — the raw file as received: raw_data_type (how R reads it), raw_data_format, and profiling (raw_first5, raw_duplicated).
  • stable_ — the governed CSV after cleanup: stable_data_type and stable_data_format (the unit is recorded in dd_data_unit). These describe the data as it currently is.
  • desired_ — the intended interpretation, which does not change across file versions: desired_data_type and desired_data_class (a dotted family.type coordinate such as period.year or id.geographic).

Between the stages sit two rule columns, and each takes its own family of rule name:

  • raw_to_stable_transform — the lossless reformat (standardize weird dates to ISO, strip thousands separators, restore a dropped leading zero). Its job is to produce a canonical governed CSV that every tool reads correctly. Takes a read_* rule: read_mmddyyyy, read_ein, read_yyyymm.
  • desired_data_import_rule — the coercion that reads the governed column into the desired R type. Takes an as_* rule: as_id.

Which bridge closes the gap? A mechanical rule

The storage a reader produces can be one of only four base types (text, number, boolean, temporal); the desired type may also be a semantic type a CSV cannot express (categorical, identifier, list). That tells you which bridge to use:

the desired type is… example close the gap with
reader-achievable (base) a date read as text reformat (raw_to_stable_transform) — make the reader hit it
not expressible in a CSV (semantic) a ZIP that is a categorical, an ID that is an identifier import rule (desired_data_import_rule) — only metadata can say it

The design goal is to push as much as possible into the reformat (it is lossless and every downstream tool benefits), leaving import rules only for the genuinely schema-dependent distinctions.

read_* and as_* rules, and their is_* guards

A rule name tells you which stage it belongs to:

  • read_<format>() ingests a value written in that format — the name states the input. These go in raw_to_stable_transform.
  • as_<type>() coerces a value into a target type — the name states the output. These go in desired_data_import_rule.

So read_ddmmyyyy() reads 15/03/2019 and returns a Date; it does not produce dd/mm/yyyy. A rule sitting in the wrong column is visible without running it.

Every rule has a matching is_* guard from the detector library, which lives in the formex package. Before read_ddmmyyyy runs, formex::is_date() checks that the column actually looks like a date; if it does not, the rule does not match the data and you get a warning instead of silent corruption. That single idea ties the system together:

  • governance — drop a rule name in a cell and it is applied;
  • safety — its is_* guard validates the precondition;
  • iteration — update_dgf() re-runs the guards against the current data and flags rules that no longer fit (because you cleaned the file).

The workflow 

library(datagoodr)

# 1. create_dgf() launches the guessers and populates the pipeline.
#    It profiles each column, runs formex over it (formex::guess_data_type
#    with the variable name as a hint), and fills in a first pass at every column
#    of the DGF -- storage, a semantic desired_data_type/subtype/class, factor
#    levels, near-unique key flags, and the rg_ profile used to render.
dgf <- create_dgf(raw_data, file = "DGF", open = FALSE)

create_dgf() does the heavy first guess; your job is to curate two things:

(a) Move the data from raw to canonical — add reformat rules to raw_to_stable_transform so the governed CSV is clean and self-describing (standardize dates, declutter grouped numbers, preserve leading zeros). This is representation only: no information is lost, the values just get written in a form every tool reads.

(b) Add semantic context — set the desired_* fields to say what each column should be, independent of how it happens to be stored. A grade coded 1–12 is categorical, not a number; a FIPS code is an identifier with class id.geographic when it is a key, and categorical with class mutually_exclusive.geographic when it is a grouping variable. This is where you encode meaning the CSV alone cannot carry.

# Edit the DGF in Excel, or programmatically:
dgf$raw_to_stable_transform[dgf$var_name == "founded"] <- "read_mmddyyyy"  # raw -> ISO
dgf$desired_data_type[dgf$var_name == "grade_level"]   <- "categorical"    # a grade is not a number
dgf$desired_data_class[dgf$var_name == "county_fips"]  <- "id.geographic"  # dotted family.type

# 2. Apply the reformat rules to a raw extract -> a canonical, governed CSV.
stable <- stabilize_data(raw_data, dgf)
write_stable_csv(stable, "data-governed.csv", dgf = dgf)

# 3. Re-profile after you have changed a type or cleaned the data.
dgf <- update_dgf(dgf, raw_data)   # re-runs guards, recomputes rg_* for changed vars

A suggested stabilizer you can preview (formex v7)

create_dgf() does not only guess the type — it proposes how to standardize the column and shows you the result before you commit. Each variable carries a machine guess in guess_* (the detected leaf as two axes, guess_format_style and guess_unit_type, with a readable guess_label like calendar {{ date :: temporal }}), a desired_* target form you can edit, and a suggested stabilizer — a read :: [convert] :: write plan resolved by formex’s transform-path search. Its effect on the first few values is previewed in stable_first5, so a mis-detected date order is visible on sight. A reformat formex cannot reach (say a fiscal-to-calendar year, with no registered converter) is reported not-transformable rather than guessed.

Executing those plans is opt-in, so the suggestion only runs when you ask:

# Apply the suggested v7 stabilizer plans (read :: [convert] :: write) to a raw
# extract. A column with a legacy raw_to_stable_transform rule keeps using it;
# the default (use_v7 = FALSE) leaves behaviour unchanged.
stable <- stabilize_data(raw_data, dgf, use_v7 = TRUE)

Why the split pays off

  • Iterative improvement. Governance is not one-shot. You clean a column, and update_dgf() reconciles the DGF with the new state — the desired_ interpretation is stable, while the raw_/stable_ storage and the rules needed to bridge to it evolve as the data improves.
  • Portability. Because stable_data_unit/stable_data_format describe the data as it is, and the desired_ fields describe intent, the governed CSV carries enough to be understood by non-R tools — and maps cleanly onto archival standards (DDI) for deposit in a repository like Dataverse.
  • No hidden magic. Every transformation is a named rule you can read, and every rule has a guard that refuses to run on data it does not fit.

Where detection lives

Type detection is not part of datagoodr. It lives in the formex package, which owns the type ontology, the is_* detector library, guess_data_type(), and fx_stabilize(). datagoodr calls it once per column and turns the answer into DGF coordinates.

For the vocabulary and the detectors, see formex’s own vignettes — The Data-Type Ontology, Data-Type Detectors, Guessing a Data Type, and Formex — at https://lecy.github.io/formex/.
